Labour fears election collapse in Scotland

Article:

Scottish Labour has published a manifesto promising to protect public spending with higher taxes as the once-mighty party struggles to stave off disaster in next week’s elections to the parliament at Holyrood.

Any campaign cheer Labour hoped to generate with its manifesto launch was quickly cooled by a new poll that showed the party trailing the Conservatives in third place.

There is also growing voter dissatisfaction with its leadership. Some in Labour fear next Thursday’s election will threaten its survival as a major political force by securing the dominance of the Scottish National party and making the Conservatives the largest opposition group. Kezia Dugdale, Scottish Labour leader, insisted she was making progress in her long-term plan to restore the party’s fortunes, saying it now had a “much clearer sense of our values” and had policies that returned it to its political roots.

The manifesto focuses on Labour’s policy of using new tax powers coming to Scotland to add 1p to the base and higher rates of income tax and to increase the top rate by 5p to 50p. Doing so will allow Scotland to shake off UK austerity and invest in education and health, it says. Labour also wants to bring the ScotRail railway franchise back into public ownership and provide breakfast clubs at state primary schools. “We all benefit from better public services and I believe people are willing to pay together to protect them and improve them, providing they know that the richest pay their fair share,” Ms Dugdale said.

The SNP plans only minor tweaks to income taxes, saying it would be unfair to raise the burden on the less well-off and that raising the top rate would risk reducing revenues if even a few of the most affluent move south or restructured their financial affairs. Ms Dugdale accused Nicola Sturgeon, Scotland’s first minister and leader of the SNP, of abandoning the role of anti-austerity champion she took on during last year’s UK general election.

“She is the one who is refusing to tax the rich,” Ms Dugdale said.

Polls suggest there could be widespread public approval for Labour’s tax policies — but that does not extend to the party.

Many traditional Labour voters accuse the party of moving too far to the right under former UK leader Tony Blair, and the SNP has also scooped up former supporters who backed independence in Scotland’s 2014 referendum.

Wednesday’s Ipsos Mori poll for broadcaster STV found only 17 per cent of respondents would back Labour in the proportional representation regional list section of next Thursday’s vote, down two points from February. The Conservatives were up four points at 19 per cent and the SNP far ahead on 45 per cent.

Almost as worrying for Labour, Ipsos Mori said Ms Dugdale’s personal satisfaction rating has suffered a -16 point swing since February and she was now the only Scottish party leader to have a negative rating.

By contrast, respondents gave the SNP relatively high marks for its record in government and a net satisfaction rating for Ms Sturgeon of 39 per cent.

The gulf in personal popularity is the main reason why the SNP is running a presidential-style campaign centred on Ms Sturgeon, issuing wristbands with the slogan “I’m with Nicola” and a manifesto dominated by the first minister’s smiling face.

“Our manifesto isn’t about the politician on the front cover, it is about the people of Scotland,” Ms Dugdale said.
